title: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
summary: Transfer Data to Cloud Account is exfiltration that stays inside the provider network: instead of pushing stolen data out to an external destination, the attacker copies, shares or syncs it into a second cloud account under their control on the same service. Because the traffic never crosses the organisation's internet boundary, network based monitoring for large outbound transfers or command and control channels can miss it entirely, and the transfers may even use internal provider addressing and ordinary provider interfaces. Common shapes include object replication or sync jobs between buckets or containers, snapshot and image copies shared with another account, disk or virtual machine backups written to attacker owned storage, and cloud native sharing features such as public sharing links or a shared access signature address that lets an outside party read a file without owning an account. The telemetry is therefore identity and control plane oriented: cross account permission grants, new sharing links, snapshot sharing records, replication and copy operations in audit logs, and unusual update or read patterns by a single principal. The reliable discriminator is the destination account, since a legitimate engineering team rarely needs to hand its data to an unrelated tenant.

beginner.definition: This technique is stealing data by moving it into another cloud account. The attacker owns that second account. The data travels inside the provider network instead of over the open internet.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many defences watch the edge of your network for large uploads. A copy that stays inside the provider never crosses that edge. Your data can be gone while your network charts look normal. Sharing links can also stay valid long after the attacker has left.
howItWorks: The attacker needs rights in your cloud account. Stolen keys or a hijacked administrator account are the usual route.
They create or own a second account with the same provider, which becomes the new home for the copied data.
They grant that account permission to read your storage, or they simply make a public sharing link.
They start a copy or sync job. A sync job keeps two storage locations matching each other automatically.
Backups and machine images are often copied too, because they hold whole systems in a single package.
The provider logs these actions on the control side. Cross account permission changes are the trail to follow.
beginner.example: Picture a post office where all sorting happens in one building. A worker does not carry parcels out of the front door. They simply relabel a sack and push it onto the trolley for a different depot inside the same building. The front door camera records nothing at all.
takeaways: Data can leave your cloud without ever leaving the provider network, so edge monitoring is not enough.
Alert on new cross account permissions and shared links, especially on storage that holds sensitive data.
Review sharing addresses that grant access without a login, and expire them automatically.

objectives: Explain how exfiltration to another account in the same cloud provider avoids perimeter monitoring.
Describe provider features such as replication, snapshots and sharing links that can move data between accounts.
Identify the audit log entries that record cross account access grants and copy operations.
Explain why a shared access link or signature address is a risk even without an attacker account in your tenant.
Describe a control that limits sharing of storage with accounts outside the organisation.
